key_insight: STEM replaces the FFN up-projection with a static, layer-local token-indexed embedding lookup while keeping gating and down-projection dense, removing runtime routing and enabling CPU-offload with async prefetch; this decouples parameter capacity from per-token compute.
problem_solved: Solves instability, load‑balancing and communication overheads of fine‑grained sparsity/routing in transformers so models can increase parameter capacity without proportional per‑token compute cost.
method: Replace the FFN up‑projection with a static, token‑indexed embedding lookup that is local to each layer.
Retain a dense gating mechanism and dense down‑projection to preserve expressive capacity and training stability.
Enable CPU offload of embedding tables with asynchronous prefetch to eliminate runtime routing and cross‑device communication bottlenecks.
impact: Makes it practical to scale transformer parameter count with lower per‑token compute and fewer routing/communication issues, improving training stability and enabling larger models on commodity hardware or CPU‑backed memory.
visual_elements: Side‑by‑side architecture diagram: standard FFN vs STEM (show embedding lookup replacing up‑projection; dense gate + down‑projection preserved).
Chart: parameters vs per‑token compute — STEM showing increased params with flat per‑token compute (compared to dense and routed sparse baselines).
Pipeline schematic of CPU offload + asynchronous prefetch illustrating reduced runtime routing and communication.
Iconized benefit strip: stability, load balance, lower comm overhead, and easier deployment on commodity hardware.
paper_title: STEM: Scaling Transformers with Embedding Modules
paper_authors: Ranajoy Sadhukhan, Sheng Cao, Harry Dong, Changsheng Zhao, Attiano Purpura-Pontoniere
